Apple rootstocks: M.9, MM.106, MM.111 and M.7

By Gafar Laiya, Gujarat Bio Organics · Updated 2026-11-25

Pick the rootstock for your soil and water first. M.9 (30–40% vigour) bears in 2–3 years and resists collar rot, but needs deep, fertile, irrigated soil, a 3–4 wire trellis and drip. MM.106 resists woolly aphid and bears early, but is highly susceptible to collar rot in wet or clay soil. MM.111 suits drier, shallower hill soil. Seedling rootstock anchors well on steep unirrigated slopes but takes 6–8 years to bear (Himachal package of practices, ICAR-CITH).

Common rootstock mistakes

  • MM.106 in heavy clay or wet soil: the main cause of collar rot deaths in young medium-density orchards.
  • M.9 on poor, dry or windy land without trellis or drip: small fruit, leaning trees and early decline, especially with spur strains.
  • Burying the graft union: keep it 15–20 cm above the soil, or the variety roots itself and loses the rootstock's benefits, and collar rot risk rises.
  • Replanting into old apple pits: replant disease stunts new trees on any rootstock except, partly, the Geneva series. How to treat replant soil.

Questions farmers ask

What is the best rootstock for apple in Himachal?

On deep, irrigated, terraced land with trellis: M.9. On well-drained slopes: MM.106 (not in clay). On drier, shallow hill soil: MM.111. On steep, unirrigated slopes: seedling.

Why are MM.106 trees dying?

MM.106 is highly susceptible to Phytophthora collar rot in wet or clay soil. Improve drainage, keep the graft high and treat as for collar rot.

Does M.9 need support?

Yes. M.9 has shallow, brittle roots and needs a 3–4 wire trellis and drip irrigation.
